originalTitle: Lofty ambitions: can puffer jackets be made more sustainable?
summary: As temperature dip, the puffer’s appeal inflates. But quality and filler are factors to consider before buying new
content: Whether you call it a parka, puffer or Tassie tuxedo, the insulated jacket has become a cold-weather closet staple. A 1920s version by Australian mountaineer George Finch was constructed from hot air balloon fabric and eiderdown, but most modern designs are a mix of petroleum-based synthetics as well as animal and plant fibres, with varying environmental and ethical impacts. Producing these materials, through agricultural or chemical processes, contributes 83% to the jacket’s overall carbon and water footprint, according to one life cycle study. The next largest contributor was water and energy usage during wear – with the average down jacket lasting seven years – followed by sewing and disposal. Natural fibres like down and wool also add animal welfare considerations. But, like all clothing items, the effects are multiplied across global production and consumption systems. The market for puffers is large and growing, with more than 100m jackets made in China annually. Some brands are even branching into new territory, with demand for puppy puffers soaring. Dr Carolina Quintero Rodriguez, a senior lecturer at RMIT University’s school of fashion and textiles, says advertising and social media are encouraging us to purchase more than we need. “That is incentivising or creating a need in the population for not only one jacket, but you need three jackets,” she says. A recent Adelaide University study of nearly 600 people’s clothing habits found 89% of garments are bought new, with padded jackets one of the most expensive items that people own, but rarely wear, which provides a ready supply of secondhand puffers in great condition. That’s why it’s important to choose a good quality garment, from a responsible brand, and wear it and repair it for as long as possible. One jacket, many ingredients Julie Boulton, a sustainable fashion consultant, says puffers usually consist of an inner and outer shell, a filler (“the stuff that makes it puff”), and notions like zips, snaps or buttons and thread. Shells are usually made from fossil fuel-derived materials, such as nylon or polyester, sometimes blended with cotton or wool. Jackets labelled “100% recycled” usually comprise polyesters made from plastic waste, such as water bottles or used textiles. The padding inside often consists of duck or goose feathers (called down), wool, or a synthetic fill, Boulton says. Some brands, like Pangaia, are moving to plant-based fluff, made from wildflowers, biopolymers and aerogel. According to the life cycle study, polyester fibre production, spinning, weaving, fabric dyeing and finishing are all high-energy consumption processes. Polyester is a petroleum-based fibre that has issues with greenhouse gas emissions and shedding microplastics, Quintero Rodriguez says. Natural down is biodegradable and a byproduct of the meat industry, she says, but can come with risks associated with animal welfare and supply chain opacity. Down is made by plucking the soft feathers of ducks or geese, usually after slaughter, according to the RSPCA, although a small percentage (1 to 2%) is still thought to be collected from live plucking, a practice the organisation says is a major welfare concern. Consumers are encouraged to look for the Responsible Down Standard, a voluntary certification that requires higher levels of animal welfare, traceability and prohibits live plucking. When it comes to wool, Dr Natalie Roadknight, a senior scientific officer at the RSPCA, says the biggest welfare concern is a practice called mulesing, which involves cutting an area of skin near the tail. “It’s done while the lamb is completely conscious,” she says. “They’re able to feel the cuts”. Australia is one of the only countries where the practice is still legal, with the procedure banned in New Zealand and other countries. Consumers can choose to avoid wool products that involve mulesing, by asking the brand directly, or looking for the ZQ Merino or the Responsible Wool Standard. Re-wear and repair Australians buy 1.5bn new items of clothing each year, and send 220,000 tonnes to landfill, a report by Seamless, Australia’s clothing stewardship scheme, has found. “If you’re thinking about getting a jacket, look secondhand, look from your friends, don’t think that you’ve got to go and buy new,” says Boulton. After that, the key is to keep it in service for as long as possible, she says. “While you’ve got it, use it, and wear it, wash it responsibly and take care of it and repair it.” Some outdoor brands offer repair services or kits to help people patch and mend their winter coats. About one in 10 items are repaired, the Adelaide University study found, even though mending extended a garment’s useful life by 2.5 years on average. Quintero Rodriguez says most garments don’t need to be washed as often as people think; sometimes, airing them out is enough. But if you do have to clean them, use cold water, she says, because heat can damage synthetic fabrics like nylons or elastane. Gentle washing can also extend the life of water resistant or repellent surfaces in raincoats, with some finishes able to be reapplied or reactivated. Can puffers be recycled? Nationally, about half of unwanted clothes end up in landfill (53%), another 38% are reused locally or exported, and 9% are recycled. Textile recycling is a time and labour intensive process, Boulton says, partly due to a lack of infrastructure and also because the price of virgin polyester is so cheap. Some outdoor brands do offer take back schemes, through places like Upparel. “It’s cheaper just to make a whole new [jacket] than it is to recover and repurpose, or deconstruct, recycle and put back into the system again, which is such a shame.” Quintero Rodriguez says: “My main message will be to extend the life of the item as much as possible. Care for the item as per the care instructions. And to make sure that you purchase [only] what you need.”
chineseTitle: 远大抱负：羽绒服能否变得更加可持续？
chineseSummary: 随着气温下降，河豚的吸引力就会增强。但质量和填充物是购买新产品之前要考虑的因素
chineseContent: 无论您称其为派克大衣、羽绒服还是 Tassie 燕尾服，这款保暖夹克已成为寒冷天气衣柜里的必备单品。澳大利亚登山家乔治·芬奇 (George Finch) 在 1920 年代的版本采用热气球织物和鸭绒制成，但大多数现代设计都是石油基合成材料以及动植物纤维的混合，对环境和道德影响各不相同。根据一项生命周期研究，通过农业或化学工艺生产这些材料占夹克整体碳和水足迹的 83%。第二大因素是穿着期间的水和能源消耗——羽绒服平均可以使用七年——其次是缝纫和处理。羽绒和羊毛等天然纤维也增加了对动物福利的考虑。但是，与所有服装一样，其影响在全球生产和消费体系中成倍增加。羽绒服市场规模巨大且不断增长，中国每年生产超过 1 亿件羽绒服。随着幼河豚的需求猛增，一些品牌甚至开始涉足新领域。皇家墨尔本理工大学时装与纺织学院高级讲师 Carolina Quintero Rodriguez 博士表示，广告和社交媒体鼓励我们购买超出我们需要的东西。 “这会刺激或创造人们不仅需要一件夹克，而且需要三件夹克，”她说。阿德莱德大学最近对近 600 人的着装习惯进行了一项研究，发现 89% 的服装都是新买的，其中衬垫夹克是人们拥有但很少穿的最昂贵的物品之一，这为二手羽绒服提供了现成的状况良好的供应。这就是为什么从负责任的品牌中选择优质服装并尽可能长时间地穿着和修理它很重要。一个插孔
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
